Artist / Group / Collective / Organizer: New Media Society, Curated by: Amirali Ghasemi, along with a group of colleagues

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Mapping Karimkhan; Mapping the Cultural and Artistic Changes in the Heart of Tehran is a participatory project that took shape with a focus on the cultural, social, and artistic changes in the Karimkhan Street area.

This project is inspired by the idea of expanded mapping; an approach that views the map not just as a physical representation of space, but as a ground for recording narratives, lived experiences, and informal knowledge.

The project began with the observation of a gradual but profound change; a change that had been happening in the Karimkhan area since the early 1990s, coinciding with the start of Rafsanjani's second presidential term.
The Karimkhan area had gradually turned into one of the focal points for cultural and artistic spaces in Tehran, attracting artists, galleries, cafes, and art audiences.

The project progressed with the participation of audiences, artists, neighbours, residents, and cultural activists, aiming to examine the process of formation, concentration, and relocation of cultural and artistic spaces in this area.
A hand-drawn wall map, TV screens, a small library with a reading area, questionnaires, conversations, and meetings were the main tools of this process.

sections.title: Context & Site
paragraphs: The project was executed in the space of New Media Projects, an independent, artist-run, and non-institutional space that provided the possibility of activities outside the official structures of power.
The choice of this space was due to its semi-public nature; a place where free conversations, voluntary participation, and the collective production of knowledge could be shaped.
On the other hand, the Karimkhan Street area itself was important as the conceptual context of the project.

Over more than two decades, this area has gradually undergone numerous changes in land allocated usage, a concentration of cultural activities, an increase in property and rent prices, and, recently, a kind of gentrification.
The project defined its relationship with these very developments and sought to examine the relationship between art, economy, the city, and everyday life in this area.

sections.title: Motivations & Questions
paragraphs: The main motivation of the project was the need to understand the changes that had occurred and were still occurring in the Karimkhan area.
The project raised questions, including: How exactly did these cultural and artistic changes take shape?
What factors led to the concentration of artists and cultural institutions in this area?
What is the role of art in these urban developments?
Do artists unintentionally play a role in the process of gentrification and the displacement of residents?
How is the current situation of the Karimkhan area in relation to the surrounding neighborhoods?
Based on global experiences, can a probable future be imagined for this region?
The project also paid attention to the issue of the "right to the city" and the social responsibility of artists towards their surroundings.

sections.title: Constraints & Strategies
paragraphs: The project faced multiple resistances and tensions along its path.
Some artists and cultural activists believed that gentrification in the Karimkhan area was not happening at a serious pace, and it was not enough to raise more attention to the issue.
In contrast, some cafe owners and cultural businesses saw the raising of these discussions as detrimental to their economic interests.
On the other hand, many neighborhood residents who later faced increased rent prices were forced to leave their homes, studios, or even leave the city.
These situations created serious conflicts of interest and disagreements.
The project's strategy for dealing with these situations was to avoid polarization and to create a space for pausing, dialogue, and co-learning.
Instead of providing definitive answers, the project tried to pose questions and provide the possibility for diverse and sometimes contradictory narratives to be heard.
The use of various media, informal meetings, and an open archive were among the main strategies of the project.

sections.title: About the Artist
paragraphs: New Media Society is an independent, non-commercial, and research-oriented collective in Tehran that began its activities in June/July 2014 (Tir 1393).
Functioning as an archive, library, and project space, this center focused on supporting media arts and fresh ideas.

The collective's mission was pursued through organizing lectures, workshops, publishing texts, and cultural residency programs, aiming to fill the academic gap while creating a constructive connection between domestic and international artists.
New Media Projects hosted many other cultural initiatives and partner collectives, giving them a platform to organise their program using its space and infrastructure.
The physical space of the New Media Projects in Tehran has been closed since Jan 2023, and it continues its journey as a nomadic /online entity.
In the first phase of the project, a large map of the Karimkhan Street area was drawn on one of the walls of the New Media Projects' common area.
The wall was painted black and often used as a blackboard / parallel archive presentation area.

From the beginning, this map was defined as an open and forming structure; a map that was not meant to be completed by a limited group, but to change and expand with the presence and with the intervention of a diverse range of people visiting the space.

The project participants included various groups: visual and new media artists, curators and cultural activists, researchers in the fields of art and the city including few architects and urban planners, residents of the Karimkhan area, passersby, people who commuted to this area for work, leisure, or daily affairs, and finally the visitors of New Media Projects who regularly visited this space for various programs.
These people participated in the project in various ways.
Some intervened directly on the map, marking active cultural and artistic locations.
Some identified spaces that no longer existed or had changed their usage.
Some added temporary, independent, or less visible places to the map; places that usually have no place in official maps or institutional archives.
Another part of the participation was dedicated to storytelling.
Individuals recorded their personal experiences of living, working, visiting exhibitions, or their daily presence in the Karimkhan area, either in writing or orally.
These narratives were sometimes accompanied by nostalgia and sometimes by criticism, dissatisfaction, or questions about urban changes.

Questionnaires were another participation tool that allowed visitors to express their views on the neighborhood's changes, the role of art, the reasons behind the Karimkhan area being so attractive for the artists, and the consequences of this concentration.
In addition, some people participated in video interviews and explained their experiences and analyses in more detail.
The project also included informal collective meetings and conversations where artists, researchers, and audiences discussed the observed trends, disagreements, and existing contradictions.

These conversations often went beyond the map itself, drawing into issues such as gentrification, cultural economy, the role of the artists in the city, and the relationship of art with everyday life.
The project space was deliberately designed in a way to allow for staying, pausing, and lengthy conversations.
People spent a lot of time in the project space, drank tea, and repeatedly returned to the map and content provided.
In this sense, participation was not a momentary act, but a continuous and repetitive process that took shape over time.

Ultimately, the wall map was the result of the accumulation of these participations; a map that recorded not only the location of places but also a network of relationships, narratives, disagreements, and lived experiences.
